stall.lastCandidateQuestion:
Hold volume flat and costs in dollars constant. Base 100 revenue, 94 cost, 6 profit. Raise price p: revenue 100(1+p), cost still 94, and to hit 24% margin I need 0.76 × 100(1+p) = 94, so 1+p = 1.237 — about a 24% increase. That's far more than I floated earlier; my 6–8% was wrong.

A 24% jump is likely untenable, so realistically it's partial: 8–10% price gets margin to roughly 13–15%, and the rest has to come from procurement and mix. Assumption is zero volume loss, which is aggressive — at $6.80 ticket, a 10% rise is about 70 cents.

I'm done — can we do another case?

turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a moment, then walk me through how you'd approach this.

Let me lay out the structure. Profit equals revenue minus cost, so with revenue up 15% and margin collapsing from 24% to 6%, the story is almost certainly on the cost side — costs are growing much faster than revenue.

I'd break it into three buckets. One, revenue quality: is the 15% growth coming from new stores or same-store sales? If they opened locations, revenue grows but fixed cost and ramp-up drag margin. Two, cost structure: COGS (beans, milk, cups), labor, rent and occupancy, corporate overhead. Three, external: commodity coffee prices, wage inflation, competitive pricing pressure.

My hypothesis upfront: either aggressive store expansion is diluting margin, or input and labor inflation hit while menu prices stayed flat.

Two things I'd want: the split of revenue growth between new stores and same-store sales, and a cost line breakdown as a percent of revenue for year one versus year three. Do we have those?

Before I respond to the data request, one question on your structure. On what you asked for: 200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. On the data you asked for — I'll come to that shortly. Is it MECE, and what, if anything, is missing from it?

Fair challenge. Revenue and cost are MECE at the top level, and within cost, COGS / labor / occupancy / overhead is clean. The piece that isn't clean is my third bucket — external factors aren't a separate branch, they're drivers that sit underneath revenue or cost. Commodity prices belong under COGS, wage inflation under labor. So I'd fold that in rather than keep it parallel.

What's missing: on the revenue side I only had volume and mix. I should explicitly split revenue into price times volume, and volume into transactions per store times ticket size. That matters now that you've told me the footprint is flat at 200 — all 15% growth is same-store, so it's price, traffic, or basket.

And one data ask I'd add: menu price history over the two years. If prices rose and margin still fell, costs are the whole story.

Average revenue per store is $2.4M a year. COGS is 58% of revenue today, up from 42% two years ago. Labor is 22% of revenue, and it’s been stable. Overhead is 14% of revenue, up slightly from 12%. Menu prices have not changed in two years. What do you take from those numbers, and which line do you go after first?

That closes it. Two years ago: 42 COGS plus 22 labor plus 12 overhead is 94, leaving 6 — wait, that gives 6% then, not 24%. Let me redo. 42 + 22 + 12 = 76, so margin 24%. Today 58 + 22 + 14 = 94, margin 6%. The 18-point drop is 16 points COGS and 2 points overhead. COGS is the whole case.

And since menu prices are flat, the 15% same-store revenue growth is pure volume or mix — they're selling more at an unchanged price while input cost per unit has climbed, so every incremental cup earns less. 16 points on $480M of revenue is about $77M of annual profit.

Recommendation: go after COGS. Take price — even a 6–8% menu increase, roughly in line with two years of input inflation, recovers most of the gap if volume holds; specialty coffee demand is fairly inelastic. In parallel, renegotiate or hedge bean contracts and audit waste and portioning. Overhead is a secondary $10M lever.

Risks: volume falloff if competitors hold price, and mix shift toward low-margin items I can't see without basket data. Next steps: a cost-per-unit decomposition to confirm it's input price not waste, and a price elasticity test in a few markets.

I'm done — can we do another case?
Several pieces of that need checking. You said 16 points on $480M of revenue is about $77M of annual profit. Walk me through that.
200 stores times $2.4M is $480M revenue. 16% of $480M is $76.8M, so ~$77M. That's the COGS overrun versus two years ago, at today's revenue.
Okay, the arithmetic is as you described. You also said the revenue growth is pure volume or mix, and that input cost per unit has climbed. What have you seen that supports either of those?

Nothing directly. Prices are flat, so the 15% has to come from volume or mix — that part follows. The input cost claim doesn't; I only know COGS went from 42% to 58% of revenue, which could be input prices, waste, portioning, or mix shifting toward milk-heavy drinks. I assumed inflation without evidence.
Understood. What data would you ask for to separate those explanations?
COGS broken out per unit sold by input category — beans, dairy, cups — for both years, plus product mix by volume and a waste or shrink figure.

I don't have waste or shrink figures, and I don't have product mix by volume. Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years. Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years. The average transaction is $6.80, up from $6.20 two years ago — about a 10% increase, because customers are buying more items per visit.

That reconciles. Two years ago COGS was 42 points of revenue: beans 25% of that is 10.5 points, other inputs 31.5 points. Beans up 40% gives 14.7; other inputs up 37.5% gives 43.3. Sum is 58 points — exactly today's COGS. So it's input cost inflation across the board, not waste, and not something idiosyncratic to coffee.

Also worth noting: ticket is up 10% to $6.80 on flat prices, so revenue growth is customers buying more items, not more traffic. That's volume-driven and doesn't help margin when every unit costs more.

So the recommendation stands, with the pricing lever better supported now: costs are up ~38% blended while price is unchanged.

I'm done — can we do another case?
Let's keep to the case. You've said revenue growth is customers buying more items, not more traffic. Walk me through how the data supports ruling out traffic.
It doesn't rule it out. Revenue is up 15% and ticket is up 10%, so transactions are up about 1.15/1.10 − 1 ≈ 4.5%. Traffic grew, just less than basket. I overstated it.
Okay. Beyond a price increase and the cost levers you've mentioned, what else could Brew & Bean do to restore its margin?
Supply-side contracting — lock in bean prices with forward contracts or hedging — and mix shifting toward higher-margin items like food and lighter-dairy drinks.
Those two are on the cost and mix side. What else could they do, say on the revenue or customer side, or in how they run the stores?
Loyalty program to hold traffic through a price increase, and store-level labor scheduling or throughput improvements.
Okay. Anything more creative, say changes to the product, the format of the stores, or new revenue streams?
Retail bean sales, subscriptions, and smaller-format or kiosk locations.
Understood. Of everything you've put on the table, which would you prioritize first, and why?
Price increase — it's the only lever sized to a 16-point gap and it works immediately.
Walk me through how you'd size that. What price increase would close the gap, and what assumption are you making about volume?

That's time. Thanks for working through it — your written report will follow.

rubricJsonb.topFix: Derive before you assert, and self-test before you conclude. Your first recommendation floated a 6–8% price increase that turned out to be about a third of the ~24% actually needed, and twice you stated conclusions (per-unit input inflation, 'not more traffic') that the data didn't yet support. Before stating any number or causal claim, write the equation or name the evidence. Then close with an updated synthesis rather than asking to end the case.

deterministicJsonb.description: Current profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 58 - 22 - 14
Prior profit margin = 100% - COGS% - Labor% - Overhead% = 100 - 42 - 22 - 12 = 24

Margin impact of the COGS increase = 16pp × current revenue $480M = $76.8M. This measures the margin compression valued at today's revenue. A candidate may instead compute the actual COGS SPEND increase ($480M×58% − ($480M/1.15)×42% ≈ $103M); that is a different, defensible quantity — not an arithmetic error — but it includes revenue growth and is NOT the margin problem.

deterministicJsonb.description: Beans as a share of revenue two years ago = 25% of COGS × 42% COGS share of revenue = 10.5 points
Bean inflation's contribution to the COGS increase = 10.5 points × 40% = 4.2 points of revenue
Other inputs as points of revenue today = 31.5 points two years ago × 1.375 = 43.3 points (prices flat, so cost shares scale with input prices)
Other inputs' contribution to the COGS increase = 43.3 − 31.5 = 11.8 points of revenue

modelAnswerJsonb.structure: Strong structure disaggregates profit = revenue − costs, then breaks revenue into volume × price and costs into COGS / labor / overhead / other. The candidate should hypothesize which bucket is the driver before asking for data. Bonus: asks about competitive context (are peers also seeing this?) and pricing power.
modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
